live_web_research.page_text: [2610.08554] Systemization of Knowledge (SoK): Human-Centered AI Safety for Youth Skip to main content Search arXiv Press Enter to search · Advanced search --> Computer Science > Human-Computer Interaction arXiv:2610.08554 (cs) [Submitted on 6 Oct 2026] Title: Systemization of Knowledge (SoK): Human-Centered AI Safety for Youth Authors: Pratyasha Saha , Yaman Yu , Yang Wang View a PDF of the paper titled Systemization of Knowledge (SoK): Human-Centered AI Safety for Youth, by Pratyasha Saha and 2 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: While HCI increasingly examines AI-safety for youth, the literature lacks a comprehensive view of what risks have been identified, how they are addressed, and whether proposed protections work in-practice. We systematically reviewed 100 empirical HCI studies involving children and youth interacting with or exposed to AI across schools, homes, care settings, and public services. Using the YAIR taxonomy for risks and the MIT Mitigation Taxonomy for countermeasures, we map which risks have been identified, whether each risk is addressed by countermeasure(s), and whether each countermeasure for that risk is implemented and even evaluated. The risk-countermeasure mapping shows that most risks are matched only with proposed/ideated countermeasures; few countermeasures have been implemented, and fewer still evaluated; and existing evaluations often measure technical performance rather than protection from harm. We identify where coverage is absent, where safeguards remain untested, and propose concrete directions for HCI research to strengthen youth AI-safety. live_web_research.page_text: Systemization of Knowledge (SoK): Human-Centered AI Safety for Youth â NOPE Insights Skip to main content Preprint Credible â Major labs, established NGOs, reputable named-author preprints Systemization of Knowledge (SoK): Human-Centered AI Safety for Youth Systematic review of 100 empirical HCI studies published 2019 to 2026 in which children and youth interact with or are exposed to AI across schools, homes, care settings and public services. The authors code each study's reported risks against the YAIR youth-AI-risk taxonomy and its countermeasures against the MIT AI Risk Mitigation Taxonomy, then map which of 36 observed risks have a countermeasure and whether it was proposed, designed, implemented or evaluated. Most risks are matched only with proposed countermeasures, and the evaluations that exist mostly measure technical performance rather than protection from harm. Read at arxiv.org (opens the original source in a new tab) Publisher arXiv (University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign; University of Washington) Published 6 Oct 2026 Added 1 week ago DOI â *]:min-w-0"> Key Findings â 750 records from CHI, CSCW, DIS, FAccT, AIES, IEEE S&P, USENIX Security and SOUPS were identified, 735 screened after de-duplication, and 100 empirical studies included. â 36 risks were observed across nine categories (behavioural and social development, mental wellbeing, toxicity, misuse and exploitation, bias, privacy, control and agency, usability and exclusion, system reliability). â Of 80 risk-countermeasure links, 40 (50%) were supported only by proposed countermeasures and 14 (18%) by evaluated ones; five of the 36 risks (14%) had no identified countermeasure. â YAIR risks with no empirical evidence in the corpus include extremist content, financial exploitation, disordered-eating content and long-term developmental effects. â Countermeasures cluster at the microsystem (parental controls, family agreements) and the exosystem (classifiers, guardrails); the mesosystem linking home, school, peers, platforms and services was nearly empty. â The authors argue that age-appropriate-design limits on engagement nudges may need to extend from interface nudges to relational nudges produced through a system's language, personality and simulated emotions. Methodology Notes Single-screener title and abstract screening by the first author with full-text consultation for borderline cases; structured extraction per paper (year, venue, technology, method, population, risks, countermeasures, countermeasure stage) distinguishing observed, participant-reported, author-anticipated and literature-attributed claims. Limitations stated by the authors: English-language work in HCI and security venues only, under-representing clinical, legal, industry and platform-safety research. Preprint v1 submitted 2026-10-06; not peer reviewed. article.body:
Youth AI safety paper maps risks and untested safeguards

Pratyasha Saha, Yaman Yu and Yang Wang’s *Systemization of Knowledge (SoK): Human-Centered AI Safety for Youth* is a review of 100 empirical HCI studies, not a user-facing product. It maps youth-AI risks using the YAIR taxonomy and countermeasures using the MIT Mitigation Taxonomy, tracking whether safeguards were proposed, implemented or evaluated. The review finds most countermeasures remain proposals, and existing evaluations often measure technical performance rather than protection from harm. This is a research synthesis, not a newly released safety capability. Availability: arXiv preprint; product access and release details are not applicable.
